content: 1. Assurance and quality improvement programs must ensure an optimal balance between high-volume centralized laboratory testing and point-of-care testing, particularly for facilities in remote locations. The use of dried blood spots is a valuable tool to enhance access to viral load testing. 2. Expanding diagnostic services to point-of-care settings requires comprehensive preparation. This includes using only high-quality, validated, and reliable diagnostic tests; supervising and monitoring point-of-care tests to ensure quality and reliability; implementing strategies for managing supply chains and equipment services; and establishing robust data management systems to promptly identify quality issues and facilitate regional and national data reporting. 3. Laboratory services should be tiered across various levels of the healthcare delivery system. This includes centralized facilities with advanced technologies for HIV molecular testing, such as viral load testing and early infant diagnosis, as well as decentralized facilities equipped with rapid diagnostic tests and point-of-care tools. 4. Comprehensive training and certification programs are essential for health workers performing laboratory tests. These guidelines should specify training requirements for specific tests and outline processes for certification and recertification. All personnel conducting point-of-care tests must be proficient in testing procedures, specimen collection, and quality assurance before service implementation. 5. A comprehensive quality management system is critical. This system should include external quality assessments, quality control measures, and standardized operating procedures for all processes, including specimen collection, test methods, result interpretation, and reporting. Testing sites must participate in external quality assessment schemes and maintain standardized logbooks or electronic data systems to monitor errors and ensure equipment maintenance. 6. Ensuring the continuous availability of high-quality, affordable essential medicines, diagnostics, and consumables at service delivery sites is a fundamental role of procurement and supply management systems. This is particularly crucial in settings with a high burden of HIV infection, where uninterrupted supplies of HIV-related health products are necessary. 7. National medicine lists should be updated to include newly recommended antiretroviral (ARV) drug regimens and formulations. This facilitates the procurement of WHO-prequalified products and ensures the availability of pediatric formulations, such as fixed-dose combinations and dispersible products, to improve adherence and supply management. 8. Efficient procurement systems must be harmonized at the national level to ensure the acquisition of quality-assured, affordable ARV drugs and diagnostics. Transparent procedures and quality assurance systems should be implemented to maintain product integrity during storage and distribution while minimizing waste from spoilage or expired products. 9. Integrated supply systems should be promoted, leveraging existing infrastructure, such as immunization cold chains, to expand the availability of pediatric formulations. Facilities must have adequate storage space, trained personnel, and tools to manage supplies effectively. 10. Robust information systems are essential for accurate and timely data on ARV drug consumption and diagnostics. These systems support effective monitoring of supply chain performance, forecasting needs, and ensuring rational use of pharmaceuticals. 11. National HIV program managers play a critical role in adapting and implementing HIV guidelines. This involves convening inclusive consultations to define necessary program changes, securing financial and political support, and ensuring accountability for implementation across all levels. 12. Human rights and ethical principles must guide the revision of national treatment policies to ensure equity and address the specific needs of all beneficiaries. New recommendations should align with the overarching vision and goals of HIV programs, integrating them into broader health and development contexts. 13. Decision-making processes for implementing global recommendations should be transparent, inclusive, and informed, recognizing the multisectoral nature of HIV responses. This approach ensures the sustainability and effectiveness of HIV programs while fostering linkages with other health and non-health programs.
